evaluation_note: Only 1 row(s): no train/test split and no cross-validation; R2 and MAE are IN-SAMPLE (measured on the rows the model was fitted on) and overstate accuracy. With n <= 3 the model has at least as many parameters as rows, so it reproduces the training rows exactly; the metrics say nothing about predictive skill. R2 is undefined (it needs at least 2 rows with different NO2 values).
sign_check: One row: no traffic effect can be estimated, the model predicts that row's NO2.

risk_comparison.comparison_note: 0 of 1 training hour(s) exceed 40 ug/m3. The sigmoid on the regression's predicted NO2 gives 0.03 (in-sample Brier 0.001); at >= 0.5 it raises 0 false alarm(s). The logistic model was not fitted (too few rows: 1 < 10). A logistic model learns only from the yes/no label, so it needs both outcomes and enough rows before it can place a boundary. The sigmoid on the regression is the more trustworthy score here: it uses every measured NO2 value rather than a yes/no label, rises smoothly with predicted NO2 (0.5 exactly where the prediction reaches 40 ug/m3) and is explained by the regression's coefficients. It is still a score, not a calibrated probability: its steepness (0.2 per ug/m3) is chosen, not fitted, and it is only as good as a regression on 1 hour(s).
